item.title: Top oil executives dropped from WPC Energy Congress amid Houthi attacks
item.description: Saudi authorities pressed ahead with the Riyadh congress despite deadly attacks claimed by the Houthis, as the kingdom outlined plans to expand its oil pipeline capacity ...
item.dc:creator: Agencies
item.content:encoded: Several top energy executives were dropped from the schedule of the World Petroleum Council (WPC) Energy Congress in Riyadh, as Saudi authorities pressed ahead with the event despite deadly attacks on the capital claimed by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis. The chief executives of ExxonMobil, TotalEnergies, Shell, Chevron and BP had all been expected at the event, which began on Sunday, but were no longer on the agenda that conference organisers released early on Monday. “To everyone who travelled to Riyadh, thank you,” said Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, who opened Monday’s session of the gathering for energy policy and industry. “You know this country is safe and that we hold your protection at whole heart…Our gathering here does not mean the risk is gone.” Prince Abdulaziz said the events of recent weeks were serious and that the kingdom’s response must be “equally serious”. The WPC Energy Congress was originally scheduled for April 2026 but was postponed after the United States (US) and Israeli war on Iran began in late February. Saudi Arabia is looking at ways to expand its oil pipeline capacity to destinations outside the Persian Gulf to 10 million barrels a day within two to three years, said Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman. The plans include improvements to pumping stations on the East-West pipeline — the key conduit for exports since the start of the US-Iran war — and repurposing a gas pipeline to transport crude, Prince Abdulaziz said. Meanwhile, air strikes targeted two districts in the Yemeni capital of Sanaa, the Iran-backed Houthi rebels reported on Monday, blaming Saudi Arabia for the strikes that occurred around midnight. A spokesman for Yemen’s Houthi-run health ministry said on Monday the air strikes killed one person and wounded 12 others. Reviewing US reply on Hormuz deal: Iran Against the backdrop of the regional conflict, Iran is still reviewing a US response to its proposal regarding the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and will reply to Washington via intermediaries when the review is over, foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday.

item.title: Russia violated energy ceasefire announced by Trump, says Zelenskyy
item.description: Zelenskyy says Russia struck energy facilities after Trump announced a truce, while Moscow rejects a 60-day ceasefire and the EU sanctions nearly 1,600 people and firms ...
item.dc:creator: Agencies
item.content:encoded: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday that Russia has continued to strike Ukraine’s energy facilities even after United States (US) President Donald Trump said a day earlier that the warring countries had agreed on an energy ceasefire in the four-and-a-half-year-old war. Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had learned through media reports that Trump had secured an energy ceasefire deal with Russia that would involve a mutual pause in strikes on energy sites. Zelenskyy said he would be willing to honour such an agreement if Moscow did the same. “We support it, but I have not heard approval of this proposal from the Russian side,” Zelenskyy said. Trump’s brief social media post on Sunday claiming the purported agreement offered few details but said that the energy ceasefire took effect immediately, adding: “Do not break it!” Yet Zelenskyy said Ukraine had been “horribly surprised” that following Trump’s “sudden but very important post,” Russia had struck numerous energy facilities, including a power plant in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, as well as a gas production facility and a civilian gas station. “It was clear that (Russian President Vladimir) Putin does not read Truth Social,” Zelenskyy said, referring to Trump’s social media platform. Meanwhile, the Kremlin on Monday rejected a 60-day ceasefire idea proposed by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to allow his country to hold presidential elections, saying it wanted an overall peace deal instead. “Please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organise elections,” Zelenskyy told ABC’s This Week on Sunday. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Monday that Russia wanted a long-term peace deal rather than a temporary ceasefire. “In the Kremlin, both President Putin and officials at other levels have repeatedly stated that we do not want a ceasefire,” said Peskov. “We want long-term peace and are prepared to do everything possible to achieve it.” Russia has long pressed Ukraine to hold elections and says that its failure to do so makes Zelenskyy an illegitimate leader. EU sanctions nearly 1,600 Russian people, firms The European Union (EU) imposed sanctions on Monday on almost 1,600 Russian people and companies linked to Russia’s arms industry, notably targeting those suspected of involvement in making parts for drones and missiles. In the biggest single listing of sanctions since the Kremlin launched the war on Ukraine almost five years ago, the EU also targeted 77 people accused of organising, working on, or running in “sham elections” in occupied parts of Ukraine. Announcing the sanctions, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said that more than half of them “address the production chain for the ballistic missiles Russia uses to kill Ukrainian civilians every day.” The EU said the companies are on a list established by the Russian government itself “that identifies them as belonging to the Russian military-industrial complex, and they are therefore entitled to receive subsidies.” The EU considers those officials running the companies to be “supporting Russia’s military and industrial complex.” It said the sanctions are aimed at “mid-level suppliers that represent the core of the Russian military industry.” The components they provide include electronics, communication equipment, radar and navigation systems, satellite and missile systems, as well as explosives and ammunition.

item.title: RBI's new forex derivatives reserve rule: Banks flag liquidity concerns
item.description: Banks warn the RBI's new 20 per cent reserve requirement on certain forex derivatives could tie up rupee liquidity, while FEDAI seeks clarity on implementation and compliance ...
item.dc:creator: Anjali Kumari
item.content:encoded: Banks have raised concerns that the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI’s) new cash reserve requirement on foreign exchange (forex) derivatives transactions could tie up rupee liquidity needed for other treasury operations. The Foreign Exchange Dealers’ Association of India (Fedai), the industry body representing authorised dealers, is taking up these concerns with the RBI and seeking clarity on how the rules will be implemented.

item.description: Trump has lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports to lower US prices, but supply limits, tanker sanctions and refinery damage could curb the impact ahead of midterm polls ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / What is the Putin-Trump diesel deal, and can it ease US fuel price pain?

What is the Putin-Trump diesel deal, and can it ease US fuel price pain? Trump has lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports to lower US prices, but supply limits, tanker sanctions and refinery damage could curb the impact ahead of midterm polls

President Donald Trump (Photo:PTI)

Reuters 4 min read Last Updated : Oct 12 2026 | 10:48 PM IST

Listen to This Article

US President Donald Trump has stepped up his efforts to lower US diesel prices by lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports and announcing a ceasefire on energy infrastructure between Russia and Ukraine.   Soaring US diesel prices are hurting US truckers and farmers, and are a concern for voters and political parties ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.   US prices were down 0.5 per cent on Monday following Trump's announcements.   How much difference will Russia's release make?   Trump said on Friday that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes (2.25 million barrels) of diesel to US and global markets. Also Read

Russia violated energy ceasefire announced by Trump, says Zelenskyy

Russia to supply diesel to US, global markets: What it means for India

EU sanctions nearly 1,600 Russians and firms over drone, missile parts

US Senators question legality of Trump's deal to allow Russian oil imports

Ukrainian Prez risks rupture with Trump as US midterms pressure mounts

That is less than a day's supply for the US transport sector alone, according to US Energy Information Administration data, which show daily use of around 2.94 million barrels.

Trump said Russia would supply another 500,000 tonnes in November and a further 1 million tonnes "immediately thereafter", which is less than four days' demand for US transport.   What hurdles might there be?   The US has lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports, but it remains unclear which tankers could be used to export the fuel, given sanctions on many of them, and what condition Russian refineries are in following recent Ukrainian attacks on them.   How much can Russia export?   Russia was capable of exporting about 100,000 tonnes of diesel a day before Ukrainian drone attacks on refineries began in 2024.   In light of damage to its refineries, Russia banned diesel exports from July to meet domestic demand and extended that ban to countries without bilateral agreements until October 31, while sustaining steady exports to "friendly" states, mostly in Central Asia.

If Ukraine halts attacks on Russian refineries, Russia would be capable of meeting the initial request from Trump for 300,000 tonnes of diesel exports, according to industry sources.   Russia could produce 300,000 tonnes of diesel this month if a large oil refinery hit by drones in the European part of the country were to restart, the sources said.   Will more diesel exports help Russia's economy?   According to Russian President Vladimir Putin, Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries cost Russia's economy 1 per cent of gross domestic product, which is around $26.6 billion, according to Reuters calculations.   Exports of 300,000 tonnes of diesel would fetch roughly $400 million, of which a small portion would go to Russia's state budget. Russia taxes mostly oil output, not oil and fuel exports.

Russia has around 30 large oil refineries, while none are functioning in Ukraine.   What’s been the reaction to Trump's announcements?   Moscow said on Saturday it had partially lifted the ban on diesel exports in place since July with immediate effect.   Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Trump's diesel supply deal with Russia would embolden Moscow's attacks on Ukraine and cost more lives.   US lawmakers also criticised the move, including one of Trump's fellow Republicans, Representative Don Bacon, who said it was time to apply more sanctions that Congress had recently passed, not lift them.   British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said his country would strengthen its sanctions on Russia. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul restated Berlin's support for Ukraine’s leader after Trump called for his removal, and called for more pressure to be put on Russia to resume peace talks.

The Kremlin said on Monday the talks were continuing on the ceasefire, while declining to comment on whether it relates only to oil refineries.   China's impact on diesel   China is set to resume refined fuel exports after a brief halt during the Golden Week holiday, Reuters reported.   However, its approved October exports of diesel, petrol and jet fuel, at around 3.7 million tonnes, are down sharply from a year earlier and lower than the more than 4 million tonnes approved for September.   Why have diesel prices been so tight?   In addition to Russian export challenges, the Iran war has curbed supply from Gulf producers.   IEA spurring more supply

The Group of Seven nations agreed recently to release fuel from their strategic reserves, coordinated by the International Energy Agency.   The 32-nation IEA coordinated the world's largest emergency stocks release in March of over 400 million barrels of crude oil and products, and has recently prodded participating countries to offer any unreleased volumes to the market.
